scientific_interpretation: Both Groq and OpenRouter were semantically stable and protected-correct on EXP-C-004, supplying a useful stable-correct control. However, OpenRouter required roughly two orders of magnitude more observed latency than Groq for the same five-sample calibration. This reinforces that review-trigger quality must be evaluated jointly with latency/cost, not accuracy alone.
design_consequences: Retain provider-specific latency as a first-class EXP-K routing signal.
Do not infer reviewer quality from speed or vice versa.
Stable-correct controls are required when calibrating semantic escalation to measure unnecessary review overhead.
Provider/model selection should eventually be task-specific and cost/latency aware after qualification, not globally ranked.
limitations: One case does not establish provider-level accuracy.
Observed OpenRouter latency may reflect free-tier/provider queue conditions and must not be generalized without more samples.
No production semantic threshold is inferred.
